_comment: Due dates for each week's case study. The quiz gate reads this to decide what is overdue,
which is what lets a green check mean 'everything due so far is done' instead of merely
'nothing detectably wrong'. Times are 11:59pm America/New_York on the date given.
Weeks not listed here are not checked until they have a BRIEF.md. Add weeks 7-15 as their
`brief` holds each week's brief: the audience it is written to and the questions the
student answers. It is the single source for three things - scripts/new_brief.py writes
weeks/weekNN/BRIEF.md from it, the agent reads it to scope the analysis (see CLAUDE.md),
and the week's deck reads it so the slide and the repo cannot drift. Editing a question

week01.title: Entropy in the NFL
questions: How did you define success in short yardage, and why that measure?
Do you see a trend between standardized entropy and your measure of success?
What other information would you want to look at to determine how important entropy is for success?
How would you go about assessing the optimal entropy for a given team?

week02.title: Which kickers can you actually tell apart?
questions: Which kickers, if any, can you separate from league average, and what test did you use to decide?
Brandon Aubrey made 40 of 47 attempts and finished 17th of 31 kickers in FG%. Your GM wants to replace him. How would you advise your GM?
How much does adjusting for the distances a kicker was sent out from change the ranking, and who moves the most?
Does adjusting for distance change your answer about Aubrey? Say why in two sentences.
Create a visual comparing Aubrey to other kickers around the league.
Which kicker do you believe is the best in the league? What other data do you wish you had to answer that question?

week03.title: Is Jorge Polanco's April real?
questions: Before a single at bat in 2025, what were the odds Polanco would hit .300 this season, and where did that number come from?
After April, how likely is it that he is a .300 hitter rather than his career .263? Show me the two likelihoods behind the answer, using his 28 hits in 73 at bats.
Run the same computation on every hitter in the data who hit .300 or better in April with at least 50 at bats. Who tops the list, and how many of them should we believe?
How much does the answer depend on the prior? Show it at 1% and at 50%.
Give me one visual that shows why the same April average is stronger evidence for one hitter than for another.
What else would you want to know before changing the lineup?
